The game everyone else plays

Before you look at our numbers, look at the game every other kind of advertising makes you play. It comes in three flavors — and every one of them is built for big companies, not a one-man lure operation.

Flavor 1 — Pay per click

You bid against everybody else for the same eyeballs, and you pay every time somebody clicks your ad. On Google's Display Network that runs about $0.63 to $1 a click (2025 benchmarks). Some of those clicks are real customers. Some are fat thumbs, bots, and accidents — and you pay for all of them the same.

The small-maker problem: the click is only the start. You need a website built to convert, ad creative that stops thumbs, keyword work, and somebody babysitting the bids every week — plus a test budget of hundreds a month just to learn what works, while you're bidding against companies with marketing departments.

Flavor 2 — Pay per thousand impressions

Don't want to pay per click? Pay every time your ad blinks past somebody — about $3.12 per thousand impressions on the Display Network. The average click-through rate is 0.46% (WordStream, 2025): out of 200 people who "saw" your ad, not even one clicked. And about a third of US internet users run ad blockers — a chunk of the impressions you paid for never existed in the first place.

Flavor 3 — Pay per install

Brands pay for every phone that installs their app: $2.50 to $5.00 a pop in North America (2026 benchmarks). Sounds clean — until you see what happens next. About one in four people open the app the day after installing. After a month it's single digits, around 4–7% (UXCam / Adjust, 2026). You paid for a hundred installs and ninety-some are gone.

The punchline

All three need the same things a small lure maker doesn't have: a marketing funnel, creative that converts, somebody managing it every month, and a budget big enough to survive the learning phase. The game is built for big companies.

Sponsor tiers & pricing

Four tiers. Higher tiers include everything below. All commitments are paid upfront — no monthly billing, no chasing payments. Two doors in:

CommitmentHow it works
12 months upfront10× the monthly rate — two months free. The standard pitch and the best per-month price.
6 months upfront6× the monthly rate — no discount. One season, the low-risk way in.

No month-to-month. A sponsor who's paid upfront is invested — no tire-kickers, no churn, no accounting headache.

Founding = first ten sponsors, rate locked forever.

Calibrated against real print: even the smallest local weekly newspaper charges $100+/week ($400+/month) for a small ad — general readers, seen once. Tier 1 at $100/mo puts a maker in front of targeted trappers daily, all season, with a tap straight to their site. Pitch line: "For less than one week in the local paper, you're in every trapper's pocket for a month."

Rotation & exclusivity

Same placement, two doors in. All paid upfront — 12-month or 6-month terms only. No monthly billing, ever.

ModelHow it worksPrice

Rotation weeks are scheduled in advance; first-paid picks their weeks. Rotations are first-paid, first-served — no competitor exclusions. They're all competitors; if somebody has a genuine problem sharing a rotation, they raise it and Tanner settles it case by case.

How shared rotation runs (operating procedure)

StepWhat happensWho does it
1. Sign upSponsor pays upfront (12-mo or 6-mo) for a shared tier. They're added to that placement's queue in the order they paid.Muse keeps the list
2. Rotation startsNo waiting for four. Whoever's paid rotates — 2 sponsors alternate weeks, 3 rotate three ways, 4 rotate four ways. Everyone gets equal time; the placement never sits empty.Automatic
3. Weekly swapSponsor 1 owns week 1 of each month, sponsor 2 owns week 2, and so on. Static all week, changes Monday morning. No reshuffling, ever.Automatic
4. Renewal / exitWhen a sponsor's term ends, the next payer on the waitlist slides into their week slot. Non-renewals are backfilled first-come, first-served.Muse manages the queue
5. ConflictsThey're all competitors — nobody is excluded from a rotation. A genuine dispute gets raised and settled case by case.Tanner settles genuine disputes only

Upgrading from shared to exclusive

Upgrades take effect at renewal, not mid-term — nobody who's paid ever gets bumped. When a shared sponsor's term is up, they get first dibs on buying their tier outright before the slot opens to anyone else. The one exception: if a rotation has only one paid sponsor in it, they can upgrade on the spot — unused shared months credit toward the exclusive price, and the new 6- or 12-month term starts that day.

Tanner's involvement: cash the checks. Everything else — the waitlist, the schedule, the Monday swaps, the backfill — runs without him. He gets a periodic note on who's in each rotation.

The pitch

How it's sold

Open with the audience story (your brand in a trapper's pocket, daily, all season — right when he's choosing what to buy), then close on the tiered placement model — the actual buy. It works like magazine advertising: pay by placement size and exposure. The Trapper's Post print rate card is the anchor: $100–150/mo in-app undercuts a small recurring print ad in the #1 trapping trade paper.

Founding sponsor offer: the first ten sponsors lock founding rates forever and get a free logo listing during beta. Pine Hollow is founding sponsor #1. Once a sponsor's products are in the app, every demo and teaser video shows their branding — and they advertise Opossum Foot back by running the app with their own name in it. Cross-promotion both directions, no ad spend either side.

Personalized previews: for any prospect, pull their real product lineup and generate a preview page showing their brand inside the app's pickers — walk into the pitch showing them what they'd look like.

Is it worth it? Run the numbers

  • The dollar-a-day math. Tier 1 shared is $350 a year — that's $0.96 a day, less than a dollar. Tier 1 exclusive is $1,000 a year, $2.74 a day.
  • The bottle math. A bottle of quality lure runs $8–15. $350 is about 25–35 bottles. If the app sells you three dozen bottles in a year, it's paid for itself.
  • The exclusivity kicker. A full-page Fur Taker ad is $195 an issue — $2,340 a year — and it shares the magazine with every competitor's ad. Tier 1 exclusive is $1,000 a year and makes you the ONLY bait/lure brand in the dropdown. Less than half the price, none of the competition.
  • The seasonality point. Oct–Jan is when trappers buy, and the app is in their hands daily during buying season. A magazine ad in July reaches nobody who's buying.
  • The free bonus. The Scorecard ranks what catches by real numbers — and rankings can never be bought. If your product performs, you get earned visibility that money can't buy. The sponsorship is just the paid presence on top.
  • What if you do nothing? Then your competitor's logo is the one in the dropdown when a trapper logs a set.

The low-risk way in: the 6-month shared term is $210 — one season. If it doesn't move product, walk away.

Where the advertising money went

Not hype — just the numbers, with sources:

  • $203 billion. US mobile ad spend in 2024 — two out of every three digital ad dollars. (eMarketer)
  • $258.6 billion. US digital ad revenue in 2024, up nearly 15% in a single year; roughly $300 billion in 2025. (IAB / PwC)
  • $1 trillion. Global ad spend forecast to pass that mark in 2026, with 68.7% flowing through digital. (Dentsu)
  • 69%. Share of all digital media time spent on phones. (Comscore)
  • $4.01 billion → $2.46 billion. US magazine print ad revenue, 2024 to 2028 — falling about 12% a year. 2025 was the year digital magazine ad revenue was expected to pass print. (Marketing Charts)
  • The honest nod to print: 46% of US adults trust print ads more than digital; only 3% favor digital. (Hopkins via eMarketer) Print wins on trust — mobile wins on where the eyeballs actually are.

"I'm not asking you to quit your magazine ad. I'm asking where the trappers went — they're on their phones, in the woods, deciding what to buy. This puts your brand in the phone at that exact moment."

Why in-app beats both: print's credibility comes from context, not tracking — readers trust it because the ad is there for the subject, not because they were followed around the internet. Opossum Foot works the same way: your brand shows up when a trapper is logging a set and choosing bait — pure context, zero tracking. No accounts, no cloud, nothing phoning home.

Hard rules: sponsors never hear operating costs. Dropdowns stay honest — freehand entry always open. Catch data stays honest even when it embarrasses a sponsor. Scorecard rankings are earned from real catch data — never bought. Trap locations are never for sale; reports are aggregated and anonymized.
